COP31 in Antalya exposed a widening gap between formal climate negotiations and practical action: countries failed to agree on fossil fuels and finance, but coalitions of governments, companies, and civil society advanced measurable commitments. For business, the lesson is to act through both policy engagement and implementation.

Negotiations stalled, but voluntary coalitions kept movingAround 90 countries rejected the Antalya Pact, underscoring political division. Yet more than 75 countries, including China, backed a voluntary target to raise electricity’s share of energy use to 35% by 2035.

Electrification gained the investment machinery needed for deliveryThe pledge came with utilities’ plans for at least $156 billion annually in grids, renewables, and storage—evidence that coalitions can pair high-level targets with infrastructure and financing commitments.

The economic case for transition is becoming more urgentData-center power demand could exceed 945 TWh by 2030, while fossil-fuel importers incurred an estimated $330 billion in extra costs after strikes on Iran, highlighting energy-security exposure.

Businesses should implement now while shaping the rules for COP32Leaders should support national electrification plans, collaborate on credible carbon pricing and concessional finance, and assess climate vulnerabilities. Strong policy capabilities can turn fragmented regulation into competitive advantage.

The COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye made progress through coalitions of governments, businesses, and civil society under the Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA), even as negotiators failed to reach consensus on core issues such as fossil fuels and finance.The summit's main political decision, the "Antalya Pact", was rejected by around ninety countries, though some technical decisions were adopted.Meanwhile, electrification showed what coalitions can achieve. While negotiators argued over whether an electrification goal should be explicitly tied to clean energy, more than seventy-five countries, including China, backed a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption from 23% today to 35% by 2035.

The So What
“While negotiators could not reach agreement on the core issues, COP31 still showed real progress is being made through the Global Climate Action Agenda established at COP30,” says Edmond Rhys Jones, who co-leads BCG’s Center for Climate and Sustainability Policy and Regulation.“Ultimately, we need both tracks. Coalitions can move faster, but they depend on the negotiations to set the direction and bring everyone along. But a vibrant Action Agenda that shows what works and what is needed can help get negotiations back on track.”Importantly, COP31 didn't just launch the electrification pledge; it also delivered a package of supporting measures. These include utilities' plans to invest at least $156 billion a year in grids, renewables and storage, nearly $95 million in catalytic finance aiming to mobilize more than $1.2 billion of private investment, and a new IEA-led mechanism to track progress ahead of COP32.New efforts under the GCAA included a Global Zero Waste Alliance and a UNIDO-hosted agenda for green industrialization. Existing initiatives also advanced: Brazil presented its deforestation roadmap, called for by 93 countries at COP30; philanthropies announced $480 million for action on methane and other super pollutants; regenerative agriculture programs now cover 66 million hectares; and the coalition on compliance carbon markets grew to 13 members.COP31’s Summit came during a year where the impacts of a changing climate are clear.2026 is set to be one of the hottest years on record, and a strong El Niño already under way could make 2027 hotter still.The UN says it is now inevitable that the world will exceed 1.5°C of global warming and urgent action is needed to limit the overshoot.It also comes at a time when the energy transition is especially critical.Data center electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030, according to the IEA.Fossil fuel importers are estimated to have paid a gross extra cost of $330 billion for seaborne crude oil, oil products, and LNG in the six months after the strikes on Iran, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.There were over 90,000 registered participants and almost 200 government parties at COP31 which brought public and private sector leaders together to advance collective action on the energy transition, climate adaptation and resilience, climate finance, and protecting nature.“Despite the clear challenges, it was encouraging to see business leaders take ownership of the agenda through the Business Forum and the GCAA. The meetings gave businesses the chance to discuss regulations and policies with government representatives, By working together, they can speed up effective implementation and unlock green business opportunities,” says Batu Yigit, who leads BCG's energy work in Türkiye.“However, the work ahead is significant and there needs to be progress in the following areas: strong, coherent carbon pricing in line with national decarbonization goals; effective concessional finance for emerging nations; and investment in the necessary infrastructure such as electricity grids.”“It is vital that business leaders keep contributing to these discussions also at the national level, so that regulations enable decarbonization opportunities that stand up as solid investments.”Now What
COP32 will be hosted in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia in November 2027.Before then, business leaders should:Push ahead with the implementation of the priorities and pledges agreed at COP31, for example, by contributing to the development of national electrification programs.Continue to work with the wider ecosystem and coalitions to help shape supportive regulations and policies.Lean into upcoming initiatives for collective action such as the global stocktake.Businesses should also take a careful look at the climate risks facing their operations and business models and invest to reduce some of those vulnerabilities.This may include developing strategies that will help them pivot in the face of increased policy volatility and fragmentation. Enhanced policy capabilities can be a source of competitive advantage for companies who are proactive and understand all options and risks.
